extracted.intended_audience: Researchers/authors (and reviewers) conducting ML-based scientific studies across disciplines
extracted.subtask_description: A cross-disciplinary reporting checklist for studies that use machine learning methods, covering evaluation, model selection, leakage prevention, metrics and uncertainty, and external validity. It is intended to guide how to conduct and report ML-based science to improve reproducibility and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate models on test data separate from training and model selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of ML models must be done on test data separate from training data and any data that was used in model selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure reproducibility and verify validity, report how data were split and used (e.g., using a holdout test set, an external validation test set, or (nested) cross validation). Report the sample size within each split of the data, including the number of samples of each class for classification tasks. Avoid testing models on data used for selection, which can produce overoptimistic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report data split details and sample sizes per split/class
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should report how models are evaluated: For example, using a holdout test set, an external validation test set, or (nested) cross validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the sample size within each split of the data and the number of samples of each class for classification tasks so readers can assess evaluation validity and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection method
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should report how the final model(s) reported in a paper are selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the model selection process (hyperparameter search, choice among model families, selection criterion). Do not test multiple models on the holdout set and choose the best on that same holdout (this leads to overoptimistic performance). When less data are available, use nested cross-validation or maintain a separate test set. Note predictive multiplicity: different models with similar accuracy can differ on fairness, interpretability, and predictions for individuals; discuss such concerns and choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperparameter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of hyperparameters is part of the model selection process and should be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report details of hyperparameter search (what was searched, ranges, search strategy). Recognize that hyperparameter optimization can substantially affect reported accuracy and that variance in performance depending on hyperparameters can mislead model comparisons. Mention that the effect of hyperparameter optimization varies by model type and may influence model choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the performance of a model to baselines, and detail how baseline models were trained and how the baseline methods are optimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure baselines use comparable model selection and optimization procedures; otherwise baselines can be 'weak' and make new methods appear better than they are. Describe baseline training and optimization methods explicitly. See also recommendations on appropriate statistical tests for model comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain train-test separation to prevent leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: When information from the test set is used during the training process, it leads to overoptimistic performance results due to data leakage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not perform preprocessing or oversampling before splitting into train/test or CV folds. Use a held-out test set; avoid relying solely on in-sample fit. Report and justify how train-test separation was maintained. Examples include oversampling before partitioning (which inflates performance) or normalizing training and test data together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dependencies and duplicates between datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets may contain dependencies (e.g., multiple samples from the same patient) or duplicates that can produce overoptimistic results if split randomly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure train-test split or CV splits respect dependencies by placing all samples from the same unit (patient, time block, location) in the same split or fold. Use blocked CV for time series, meta-segmented CV for neighborhood/time dependencies, or other block CV strategies for temporal, spatial, or hierarchical structures. Avoid Frankenstein datasets that combine sources and inadvertently duplicate samples across splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature legitimacy (avoid proxy/leaky features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that features used in a model are legitimate and not proxies for the outcome variable, which can produce leakage and inflated performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize features for temporal or causal illegitimacy (e.g., using prescribed drugs or post-diagnosis actions as predictors). Large feature sets increase the risk of including illegitimate features; document reasoning about feature inclusion and availability at prediction time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify choice of performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must reason why the metrics used are appropriate for the task and scientific claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain metrics (e.g., accuracy) can be misleading under class imbalance; other metrics (e.g., AUROC) have limitations. Choose metrics relevant to application costs (e.g., false positives vs false negatives) and justify them relative to the scientific claim being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report uncertainty estimates for performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating and reasoning about uncertainty in performance metrics is important but under-reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify uncertainty from sampling and training variability (e.g., confidence intervals, bootstrapping within the test set). Use relevant statistical methods from analogous areas (diagnostic testing/biostatistics), consider McNemar’s test and analytic sample-size calculations for subgroup auditing, and propagate uncertainty to downstream analyses where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate statistical tests for model comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical testing can be used to evaluate differences in performance between models, but tests must be appropriate for the comparison and may not always be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reporting uncertainty over significance testing alone because reliance on significance has led to misinterpretations. If statistical tests are performed, choose tests suitable for the setting (see literature overviews) and report limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss external validity and generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should discuss the extent to which findings generalize from the sample to the target population and to other populations, outcomes, and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider threats to external validity (dataset shift, shortcut learning, temporal drift) and distinguish among claims about observed patterns, fitted models (domain generalization/robustness), and learning algorithms (algorithmic usefulness across contexts). Explain how evaluation samples map to intended real-world deployment populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence of external validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss or demonstrate the ability to generalize claims using quantitative and theoretical approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test claims on out-of-distribution data when possible, and/or make theoretical arguments referencing prior literature about similarity of contexts. Report risks of temporal drift and other causes of degradation and, when possible, include quantitative external-validation experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: State contexts in which findings are not expected to hold (constraints on generality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify circumstances under which scientific conclusions or model performance are not expected to hold to set realistic expectations and avoid hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit 'constraints on generality' or limitations statements that identify boundaries of applicability. This helps accurate interpretation, replication, and follow-up studies testing generalization to new populations.
